papers.title: Nanotechnology-Based Drug Delivery for Parkinson's Disease: A Review On Strategies, Efficacy and Translational Hurdles.
papers.abstract: Treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD) faces two significant challenges: first, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and second, a therapeutic strategy that alleviates symptoms instead of stopping the disease progression. The BBB prevents over 98% of small-molecule drugs, leaving neuroprotective options mostly inaccessible. Nanotechnology is being developed to overcome existing limitations, paving the way for more precise and effective delivery to the brain. This review goes beyond listing types of nanocarriers to critically synthesise our understanding of nanoparticle (NP)-based strategies for PD, evaluating their therapeutic potential in relation to the challenges of real-world application. Evidence from various systems is evaluated, from lipid-based carriers and polymeric NPs to advanced constructs such as dendrimers, to see how these might enhance brain bioavailability, support sustained release, and directly target disease processes, including alpha-synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation. The paper thoroughly examines the primary barriers to clinical application, including biocompatibility concerns, scalability of manufacturing, and an evolving regulatory landscape. Looking ahead, PD nanomedicine will focus on designing theranostic platforms with multiple functions. That future will depend upon close collaborations across disciplines to turn compelling preclinical results into practical, disease-modifying therapies.

papers.title: A new perspective in predicting fall risk in non-parkinsonian geriatric patients: the magnetic resonance parkinsonism index.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Falls are a major geriatric syndrome associated with significant morbidity and mortality in older adults. The Magnetic Resonance Parkinsonism Index (MRPI) is a neuroimaging biomarker reflecting brainstem structural alterations; however, its role in fall risk among non-parkinsonian older adults remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether the MRPI is independently associated with recurrent falls in older adults. METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 250 adults aged ≥ 65 years who underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and comprehensive geriatric assessment. Participants were categorised as fallers and non-fallers. MRPI values were calculated using segmentation-based measurements from three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate the independent association between MRPI and recurrent falls after adjustment for potential confounders. RESULTS: A total of 250 participants (171 women, 79 men) were included, of whom 103 (41.2%) had recurrent falls. MRPI values were higher in fallers than in non-fallers (13.22 vs. 12.74, p = 0.027). The MRPI was positively correlated with age, number of falls, number of medications, Timed Up and Go test time, and frailty, whereas it was negatively correlated with the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment score, grip strength, and functional status (p < 0.05). The MRPI was independently associated with falls across all multivariable models, including the fully adjusted model (odds ratio, 1.61; 95% confidence interval, 1.02-2.48; p = 0.031). CONCLUSION: The MRPI is independently associated with falls in non-parkinsonian older adults and may represent a novel neuroimaging biomarker for fall risk prediction.

papers.title: Rab GTPases and the Rabopathy framework: from synaptic trafficking to neurodegeneration via LRRK2-driven pathology.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases. This review introduces the concept of Rabopathy, a framework that connects developmental synaptic maturation defects with late-onset protein aggregation. The LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation axis is emerging as a potential common amplifying mechanism across these disorders, with the strongest mechanistic support in PD and growing implications in AD and HD. When Rab substrates are excessively phosphorylated at specific sites, vesicular transport is impaired or arrested, leading to progressive depletion of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles and the surface pool of receptors, and severe compromise of the autophagy-lysosome flux. The failure of distinct Rab sub-networks also produces disease-specific signatures, including Rab5-driven endosomal congestion in AD, Rab35-mediated α-synuclein secretion in PD, and Rab11/Rab7 trafficking collapse in HD. Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.

papers.title: Blood-Based Lipid Peroxidation and Ferroptosis-Related Markers in Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a neurodegenerative disease caused by reduced levels the mitochondrial frataxin protein. Systemic oxidative stress and iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, commonly associated with ferroptosis, have a critical role in disease pathogenesis. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to evaluate longitudinal changes of blood-based indexes of oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related molecules in adults and children with FRDA. METHODS: We measured plasma levels of 4-hydroxyl-2-nonenals (4-HNE) and hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (15-HETE), and blood concentration of glutathione (GSH), glutathione disulfide (GSSG), in 62 FRDA patients (48 adults and 14 children) and 63 age matched healthy controls. mRNA levels of major genes targeting the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) were also evaluated. Peripheral concentrations of lipid peroxidation markers and ferroptosis-related molecules were correlated with age, disease duration, and severity of ataxia signs. Clinical and biochemical evaluations were performed at baseline and at 1-year follow-up. RESULTS: FRDA patients had significantly increased levels of 4-HNE and GSSG and decreased levels of GSH, compared to controls. Children with FRDA had lower levels of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) mRNA than adult patients. At 1-year follow up, plasma 4-HNE levels remained stable, and blood GPX4 mRNA increased only in adult patient cohort. GPX4 correlated with age, disease duration, and clinical scores. CONCLUSIONS: We provide preliminary evidence of defective GPX4 expression in the early phase of the disease. Our data suggest that GPX4 may represent a biomarker for disease progression and a possible candidate target for therapeutic strategies. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Interpretable radiomics signature of the basal ganglia-thalamic circuitry for predicting PD-MCI: a multi-center study with external validation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: To develop and validate a T1-weighted imaging (T1WI)-based radiomic signature and integrate it with clinical features to construct a combined model for the early identification of cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed data from 233 PD patients, including 182 from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) and 51 from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC). Based on baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores, patients were classified into those with normal cognition (PD-NC) and those with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). The PPMI cohort was randomly divided into training (n = 127) and test (n = 55) sets at a 7:3 ratio, while the NACC cohort served as an external validation set (n = 51). Radiomic features were extracted from T1WI of the bilateral basal ganglia (globus pallidus, putamen) and bilateral thalamus. After dimensionality reduction, a radiomic model was constructed. Independent clinical predictors were identified and integrated with the radiomic signature to establish a combined model. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, confusion matrices, and F1-scores. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was employed to interpret model outputs. RESULTS: The radiomic model achieved area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.809, 0.777, and 0.776 in the training, test, and external validation sets, respectively. Multivariable regression identified the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) score (odds ratio [OR] = 1.41, P = 0.005) and resting tremor (OR = 4.11, P = 0.036) as independent predictors. papers.title: Relationship between apathy, glymphatic dysfunction, and white matter integrity in Parkinson's disease: a multimodal MRI study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Apathy is a disabling non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), but its neuroimaging correlates remain unclear. Glymphatic-related MRI metrics abnormalities and white matter microstructural damage have each been implicated in PD, yet their relationship with apathy is incompletely understood. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the relationships among glymphatic-related MRI metrics, white matter abnormalities, and apathy in PD, while accounting for affective, cognitive, motor, and treatment-related factors. METHODS: We prospectively enrolled 41 patients with PD [19 with apathy (APD), 22 without apathy (nAPD)] and 38 healthy controls (HC). Multimodal MRI quantified choroid plexus volume (CPV), perivascular space measures, DTI-ALPS, gBOLD-CSF coupling, free water (FW), free-water-corrected diffusion indices, and NODDI metrics. Tract-based spatial statistics, sparse principal component analysis, partial correlation, sensitivity analyses, and exploratory mediation analyses were performed. RESULTS: Compared with HC, PD patients showed widespread white matter abnormalities, including increased FW, fwAD, fwMD, fwRD, and ODI and decreased fwFA and NDI. APD patients showed higher FW than nAPD patients in clusters involving the corpus callosum, left superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, and other widespread tracts. Within PD, these FW abnormalities were associated with apathy severity; several associations persisted after adjustment for UPDRS-III and levodopa equivalent daily dose but were attenuated after adjustment for affective or cognitive symptoms. CPV measures were also associated with apathy-related FW abnormalities, with selected associations remaining after adjustment for MoCA or motor/medication measures. papers.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of Oropharyngeal Alignment Exercise on Swallowing Function in Neurological Disorders with Restricted Mouth Opening: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: PurposeThis single-arm pilot study evaluated the feasibility and tolerability of an oropharyngeal alignment exercise (OAE) protocol and explored preliminary changes in swallowing and mouth-opening capacity in individuals with neurological disorders presenting with dysphagia and restricted mouth opening.MethodsOf 12 individuals screened, nine participants (seven with stroke, one with Parkinson's disease, one with cerebellar granule cell neuropathy) completed three phases of eight sessions each: baseline, intervention, and follow-up. OAE, targeting head and neck alignment and postural correction, was delivered twice weekly for four weeks alongside routine rehabilitation. Feasibility was assessed by recruitment, retention, adherence, and safety. Outcomes included maximum mouth opening (MMO), the Mann Assessment of Swallowing Ability (MASA), the Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS), and the Penetration-Aspiration Scale (PAS) from videofluoroscopy. Changes were examined using participant-specific baseline ±2SD bands and group-level non-parametric tests.ResultsRecruitment was 75.0%, retention and supervised-session attendance were 100%, caregiver-reported home-exercise adherence was complete during intervention, and no adverse events occurred. papers.title: Non-Pharmacological Interventions for Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease: A Scoping Review of Delivery Characteristics and Relevance to Nursing Practice.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive impairment is common and disabling in Parkinson's disease and may progress to dementia in up to 80% of individuals. Non-pharmacological interventions are increasingly studied, but their modalities, delivery characteristics and clinical applicability remain unclear. AIM: To map and synthesise evidence on non-pharmacological interventions for cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease, characterise intervention modalities and delivery features and examine relevance to nursing practice. DESIGN: Scoping review. METHODS: Following Arksey and O'Malley's framework, two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Data were synthesised descriptively using an intervention modality and delivery characteristics framework. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature and Ichushi-Web were searched from inception to October 2025. RESULTS: Seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria; most were published after 2020. Interventions included cognitive training (n = 12) and exercise and dual-task programmes (n = 5). Four cognitive training interventions used technology-assisted, home-based platforms. Most were delivered by neuropsychologists or physiotherapists in facility-based settings; only one was nurse-led. CONCLUSIONS: Non-pharmacological interventions for cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease are largely non-invasive and involve structured cognitive, physical or technology-assisted components. The scarcity of nurse-led interventions highlights a critical evidence gap and underscores the need for nurse-led and nurse-coordinated cognitive care models. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Nurses are well positioned to support, coordinate and monitor non-pharmacological cognitive and exercise-based interventions for people with Parkinson's disease,

papers.title: Severe Motor Deterioration of Young-Onset Parkinson's Disease in Pregnancy Following Medication Rationalisation: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) in pregnancy is rare, and there are no agreed guidelines for its management. We report a 34-year-old primigravida with a three-year history of young-onset PD who presented at eight weeks' gestation with an unplanned pregnancy. She had previously tolerated levodopa poorly, with nausea and early peak-dose dyskinesia, and before conception her symptoms were reasonably controlled on amantadine, selegiline and procyclidine. Because of the potential teratogenicity of amantadine and limited safety data for the other agents, her treatment was changed to co-careldopa (carbidopa/levodopa) with domperidone. Her condition deteriorated soon after the switch. Despite stepwise increases in levodopa to 400-450 mg/day, by 31 weeks she was wheelchair-dependent, with severe peak-dose dyskinesia alternating with "off" periods and freezing, and she relied on her husband for feeding and personal care. Other drug options and deep brain stimulation were deferred until after delivery. Her care involved neurology, obstetric medicine, obstetric anaesthesia, safeguarding midwives, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and she received thromboprophylaxis for immobility. She presented in spontaneous labour at 37+5 weeks and underwent a category 2 caesarean section under general anaesthesia, as constant tremor precluded neuraxial anaesthesia. Estimated blood loss was 750 mL. Her daughter had Apgar scores of 4, 7 and 9 at 1, 5 and 10 minutes, respectively, and weighed 2250 g (3.4th centile). Postpartum, dyskinesia and tremor temporarily prevented her from holding her baby, and trihexyphenidyl was started; her symptoms were unchanged five weeks after delivery. In young-onset PD, withdrawal of an effective pre-pregnancy regimen may be followed by significant functional decline, and previous levodopa intolerance may be a warning sign. This case highlights the importance of pre-conception counselling, early multidisciplinary planning and postnatal support.

papers.title: Association between anticholinergic burden and geriatric outcomes in older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) frequently require multiple medications with anticholinergic and sedative properties for the management of diabetes-related complications and comorbidities, and diabetes itself predisposes patients to geriatric syndromes - making this population particularly vulnerable to the cumulative effects of anticholinergic burden. AIMS: This study aimed to determine the association between anticholinergic burden and geriatric syndromes in T2DM. METHODS: This retrospective study analysed comprehensive geriatric assessments of 715 T2DM outpatients from November 2018 to August 2024. Anticholinergic and sedative drug burden was evaluated using the Drug Burden Index, Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden Scale and Anticholinergic Risk Scale. RESULTS: Among the patients with T2DM (80.63 ± 7.3; 70.3% female), 309 had no anticholinergic burden, 320 had low burden and 86 had high burden. After adjustment for dementia, Parkinson disease and HbA1c, high anticholinergic burden was significantly associated with lower scores on the Barthel Index (P = 0.003; adjusted β = -10.22), Mini Nutritional Assessment (P = 0.005; adjusted β = -1.84), Mini-Mental State Examination (P = 0.001; adjusted β = -2.59) and the Tinetti test (P = 0.006; adjusted β = -2.11), as well as higher Timed Up and Go scores (P = 0.001; adjusted β = 5.13) and an increased risk of sarcopenia (P = 0.031; adjusted odds ratios = 1.83). CONCLUSION: Anticholinergic medication exposure is observed in more than half of older adults with T2DM. Increased anticholinergic burden is an independent risk factor for sarcopenia, malnutrition and gait, and cognitive and functional decline in older T2DM patients. The use of anticholinergic drugs in older patients with T2DM should be carefully evaluated and strategies to minimise exposure implemented.

papers.title: Critical advances and translational bottlenecks of gut microbiota-gut-brain axis targeted therapy for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.
papers.abstract: Neurological diseases have become a major global public health burden. Existing central nervous system-targeted therapies can only alleviate clinical symptoms but fail to halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, presenting mechanistic limitations and therapeutic bottlenecks. The gut microbiota participates in the regulation of central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and neuropathological processes via the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA). Notably, dysbiosis may induce damage to the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and immune imbalance, thereby mediating the onset and progression of various neurological diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease (AD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and multiple sclerosis (MS). This article provides a systematic review of the core mechanisms by which the gut microbiome regulates neurological diseases, including inflammation regulation, oxidative stress responses, and neuroendocrine remodeling mediated by microbial metabolites. It also comprehensively summarizes the research progress, application advantages, and existing limitations of novel gut-targeted interventions, such as probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), dietary interventions, and live biological therapies. At the same time, the article critically examines key bottlenecks prevalent in the field: the causal relationship between the microbiota and disease remains unclear; there is a significant translational gap between animal and human studies; there is a lack of unified standards for multi-omics analysis systems; and interference from confounding factors such as age, diet, and medications is significant. Existing research indicates that gut microbiota interventions complement traditional symptomatic treatments and hold promising prospects for early disease intervention and adjunctive therapy for refractory patients. Future efforts should integrate multi-omics and artificial intelligence technologies

papers.title: Comparative efficacy of gut microbiota-targeted therapies for motor and non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gut dysbiosis may contribute to Parkinson's disease (PD) through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Probiotics, synbiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) have been studied as potential treatments, but their comparative effects remain uncertain. METHODS: We searched trial registries and electronic databases from inception to April 1, 2026 for randomized controlled trials of gut microbiota-targeted therapies in PD. We performed a frequentist network meta-analysis. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2, and confidence in the evidence was assessed with CINeMA. Treatment rankings were summarized using SUCRA values. RESULTS: Nineteen RCTs involving 1,156 participants and five treatment options (FMT, probiotics, synbiotics, routine care, and placebo) were included. Probiotics increased spontaneous bowel movement (SBM) frequency compared with placebo (MD = 1.93, 95% CI: 0.23 to 3.64; SUCRA = 88.3%). In the oral-administration subgroup, probiotics (MD = 2.01, 95% CI: 0.64 to 3.39) and synbiotics (MD = 1.23, 95% CI: 0.01 to 2.45) increased SBM frequency. No active treatment significantly improved MDS-UPDRS III scores compared with placebo, although synbiotics and FMT had higher SUCRA rankings. Evidence certainty was Moderate for oral probiotics on SBM frequency and Low to Very Low for motor function and quality of life. CONCLUSION: Oral probiotics improved SBM frequency in patients with PD. Evidence for motor function and quality of life was uncertain, and the higher rankings of FMT and synbiotics should be considered exploratory. Larger head-to-head randomized trials are needed. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard.

papers.title: Translating Parkinson disease genetics into clinical benefit.
papers.abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by variable progression and treatment response. Over the past three decades, genetic discoveries have reshaped our understanding of PD biology, identifying rare monogenic forms, strong genetic risk variants and a large set of common and rare genetic variants variably contributing to PD heritability. These findings led to the identification of key pathways implicated in the neurodegenerative process, including protein misprocessing, lysosomal and mitochondrial impairment, and altered immune response. In this Review, we describe the evolution of PD genetics and discuss its current clinical impact and future role in shaping precision medicine, from diagnosis and prognosis to the development of disease-modifying therapies. Genetic information is increasingly used to support clinical decision-making, improve patient counselling and identify biologically distinct forms of PD. Importantly, genetic insights are driving therapeutic innovation, enabling targeted strategies and genetically stratified clinical trials. Despite ongoing challenges such as incomplete penetrance, variable expression of disease and missing heritability across multiple ancestries, integrating genetic knowledge into research and clinical practice is accelerating the transition towards precision medicine in PD, providing a framework for more personalized care and improved patient outcomes.
